title: Space versus time
summary: Memory is a cost too: work in place, or spend memory to save time.

steps.title: Space complexity
body: Big-O also measures **extra memory**: how much an algorithm allocates beyond its input.
Reversing into a new array needs `n` extra slots: `O(n)` space. Reversing **in place** with two indices that walk towards each other needs only a couple of variables: `O(1)` space.
Watch `left` and `right` close in. Each pass swaps one pair, so the loop runs `n / 2` times.

steps.prompt: The loop condition changed to `left <= right`. What does it print?
steps.explain: The third pass has `left == right == 2` and swaps the middle with itself. Harmless, but `left < right` saves a pointless step.

steps.prompt: `int[] Reversed(int[] a)` creates `var result = new int[a.Length]` and fills it backwards. What is its extra space?
steps.explain: The new array has one slot per input item. The time is `O(n)` too.

steps.title: Spending memory to save time
body: Often you can **trade** memory for speed. To find whether an array of small numbers (0 to 9) has a duplicate you could compare every pair: `O(nÂ²)` time, `O(1)` space.
Or keep a little table of counts, indexed by the value itself. One pass fills it: `O(n)` time, at the cost of an extra array.
Watch `counts`: each value bumps the box at its own index.

steps.prompt: Complete the one-pass duplicate check for values from 0 to 999.
steps.explain: Values run 0 to 999, so the table needs 1000 slots. The second time we meet a value, its slot is already `true`.

steps.prompt: How much **extra** memory does each approach use?
items: copy into a new array, then reverse that
sum the items with one `total` variable
store every item seen so far in a `HashSet`
find the maximum by keeping the best so far
build a list of the running totals

steps.prompt: A recursive function calls itself `n` levels deep before returning. Why does that use `O(n)` space even with no arrays?
options: Every unfinished call keeps a frame on the call stack
Recursion copies the whole program each call
The garbage collector stores each result
It does not: recursion is always O(1) space
steps.explain: Each call waiting for the one below it holds its locals on the stack. Very deep recursion runs out of stack, which is why some algorithms are written with loops.

steps.title: In place, and one pass
prompt: - `void ReverseInPlace(int[] a)`: reverse the array **in place**. No new arrays, no `Array.Reverse`.
- `bool HasDuplicate(int[] a)`: values are between 0 and 999. Answer in **one pass** using a `bool[]` table.
template: Dojo.Eq("reverses an odd-length array", new[] { 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 }, dojoA);
Dojo.Eq("reverses an even-length array", new[] { 8, 7 }, dojoB);
Dojo.Eq("leaves an empty array alone", 0, dojoC.Length);
Dojo.Eq("{ 3, 1, 4, 1 } has a duplicate", true, HasDuplicate(new[] { 3, 1, 4, 1 }));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 1000; dojoI++) dojoUnique[dojoI] = dojoI;
Dojo.Eq("1,000 distinct values: no duplicate", false, HasDuplicate(dojoUnique));

forbid.message: ReverseInPlace does not create a new int array

hints: Reverse: two indices, `left = 0` and `right = a.Length - 1`, swap and move them together while `left < right`.
Duplicates: `var seen = new bool[1000];` then for each `x`: if `seen[x]` return true, else set it.
